utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Stamp, are you ready with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Nike Peraj, and he will testify regarding paragraphs 72(H)(ii) and 75(H) of the indictment. If I could repeat it, paragraphs 72(H)(ii) and 75(H) of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read allowed the affirmation that is on the card given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Stamp has some questions for you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Peraj. For the record, could you please state your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Nike Peraj. I was born on the 4th of September, 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In Ramoc village, Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you tell us in 1999, the early part of 1999, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In early 1999, I was the person in charge of operational and educational issues in the military barracks of the 52nd Brigade of the Pristina Corps. It was part of the command of the Pristina Corps: The ARBR Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it that you were a member of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, up until June 1999, for how long had you been a member of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I had been a member of the Army of Yugoslavia as of 1st November, 1975, until 11th -- 10th, 11th June, 1999, which is more than 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How did your career in the Yugoslav army come to be terminated? Under what circumstances did you part with the army?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In June 1999, the Army of Yugoslavia, according to agreement at a State level, withdrew from Gjakove barracks and from Kosova as a whole, and in those circumstances I remained in my apartment in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why did you remain and not move out of there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The main reason is that I was born in Gjakove municipality. My family was and is there, my parents, my brothers. They live in a village there. The other reason would be that in Kosova -- rather, in Gjakove, terrible crimes had been committed, many casualties in people, in property. So had I left with the Army of Yugoslavia, I would automatically been proclaimed a traitor of my own people, of my own family, and so on and so forth. I know that I never participated in any combat operation or anything else and that I never committed anything wrong personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to those crimes that you speak about and other events that occurred in Kosovo, and Djakovica in particular, did you give several statements to various entities, including to investigators of the -- this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And as far as the statements that you gave to investigators from this Tribunal, do you recall that the several statements -- these several statements were compiled into one statement which you signed on the 9th of August, 2008 -- sorry, 2006?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I remember that the main -- a summary statement was compiled of the main things, which I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I will get back to the date shortly. That statement, did you have an opportunity to review it over the last few days since you have returned here to The Hague to testify?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave could I show the witness the document with the number -- 65 ter number 02253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see the English front page is before you. Do you see where you had signed that statement? Yes, do you see where you had signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The font is very small. I cannot read it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at the English version to your left at the bottom, do you see where you signed?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can see my signature. It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's dated the 8th and 9th of August, 2006.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: 8 and 9th of August, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could just have a look at the penultimate page of that statement, please. The next to last page of the statement, I'm sorry. I think we have the last page. Could we have the one before that, page 8 -- 18, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see you also signed there above the date?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It is my signature just above the date 9th August, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is, Your Honours, certified that it had been read over to him in the Serbo-Croat language and that he accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you reviewed the statement recently, I believe you indicated, Mr. Peraj, that there were certain changes that ought to be made, so can I take you first to paragraph 67 of the statement. Paragraph 67 is page 11 of the English, and page 12 in B/C/S. Is it there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, although I think we should work for the public nature of the trial using the computer technology, but perhaps it would also assist if I just handed him the -- a copy of the Albanian translation of the statement. It might help us to proceed more efficiently, with your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. And could the Chamber mention that often witnesses have difficulty reading documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- because of the size of the print and the imprecision of the screens despite the advanced technology, and where it's intended to make some extensive use of a document, the Chamber would encourage the provision of a written copy to the witness to speed up the procedure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph 67, you say that your brother was together with VJ Major Ljubisa Zivkovic, "... and I was alone." That is the next to last sentence in paragraph 67.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I see paragraph 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to the person named there, VJ Major Ljubisa Zivkovic, is that the correct person or the correct name that should be there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No. I made a correction even earlier. I pointed out this mistake. It was not this person involved in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The name of the right person was Seregj Perovic. He was a Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it should be Captain First Class Seregj Perovic instead of VJ Major Ljubisa Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that you made the correction before and explained that -- or perhaps before I get into that, maybe I should just take you through. Is it correct that wherever we see in this statement the name Major Ljubisa Zivkovic we should substitute it for Captain First Class Perovic, Seregj Perovic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Correct, with the exception of one or two places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Let's take you through, if I may, the statement. Could we move to paragraph 68. You said: "Together with Major Zivkovic ..." Should that remain the same, or should that be "together with Captain Perovic ..."?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It should state "Perovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 70, the next to last -- sorry, next to last sentence of paragraph 70 you say: "... I had nothing to be afraid of because Major Zivkovic and myself were both two officials of the VJ army." Should that be Major Zivkovic or Captain Perovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It should state "Captain Perovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 71 begins: "Together with Zivkovic ..." What should that state?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: "Together with Perovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 72, again, in the first sentence you refer to Major Zivkovic. What should that state?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It should be substituted with "Captain Perovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And again in paragraph 73, on more than one occasion you refer to Major Zivkovic. What should that say there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Again, "Perovic." "Captain Perovic," not the major.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, if we look at paragraph 75, on several occasions there are references to Major Zivkovic. What should that state in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: "Captain Perovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you now go to paragraph 76. In the first sentence, you refer again to Major Zivkovic. What should be there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Again, "Captain Perovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in paragraph 77, on two occasions you refer to Major Zivkovic. What should be there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: "Captain Perovic" on both occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in paragraph 78, in the last sentence -- well, on two occasions, in the second and in the last sentence you refer to Major Zivkovic. What should be there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: "Captain Perovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in paragraph 79, again, in the first sentence you refer to Mr. Major Zivkovic. What should be there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Again, "Captain Perovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And finally in this regard, in paragraph 81 you again refer to Major Zivkovic. What should be there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: "Captain Perovic" again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that in many -- or not many, in the earlier statements you had given to the OTP in regard to your activities in the period relative to the indictment, particularly on the 27th and the 28th of May, you had said that you were along with Major Zivkovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That's correct. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for the -- you explained for the first time in the -- during the Mos -- sorry, during the trial of Mr. Milutinovic and others in 2006, that actually it was not Major Zivkovic but it was Captain Perovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. That's what I had said. I provided an explanation, and I am ready to provide even a broader explanation if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell the Court -- well, explain to the Court why it is that in the earlier statements you had substituted Major Zivkovic for Captain Perovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: May I give you the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please, please. Explain to the Court.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: There are several reasons. The first and main reason for me doing this was of humanitarian nature, because this person helped around 100 persons to survive, and these persons live to this day thanks to him. Secondly, after the war, in 1999, the person in question, Captain Seregj Perovic, called me on the phone and asked me not to mention his name if I wanted him to live. And in the end of that conversation he repeated several times, Please, please, just forget my name; you know and I know that we both tried our best, did the impossible for as many people possible to survive and escape death, but that was all war, and that's what we could do in those circumstances. This was the main reason why I did this, and I do admit it in case you consider me for a person who did something wrong. Secondly, Major Zivkovic was informed and was in all these locations that I mentioned, that I visited with Captain Perovic, because of his function at the time. He was a member of a 3-member commission that was established for mopping up the terrain, for cleansing the terrain from the bodies and cattle that were killed in order to prevent the spreading of diseases. I was also with Major Zivkovic on every location that was bombed by NATO aircraft because I was familiar with the terrain, and that's why he wanted me to accompany him always, and to measure using a detector the presence of chemical or biological toxins, because he was a professional. He was an expert on these things, chemical weapons and biological weapons, biological and chemical defence. If I can add just one thing. I was with First Class Captain Seregj Perovic in Nec, Duzhnje, Meje, Qafe e Osekut. I have mentioned all these name. I could bring here over a hundred witnesses who have seen me with him, and the people whose lives were saved ask me even today whether I have contacted him, and they asked me to thank him for what he has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: So that is the reason why I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that Major Zivkovic was present at many of the locations that you have mentioned in your statement. Was he present at this -- these locations on the 27th and the 28th of April when you and Captain Perovic went to these locations?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Correction: No, he was not with me and Perovic. I think he went there after us because we discussed this together, and he said, I asked you -- I wanted you to come with me, but I heard that you had gone there before with Perovic. And this is the truth. This is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could return to the statement that you have in front of you and go to paragraph 6 thereof. You see in the second sentence, it is written here: "Colonel Milos Djosan was also responsible for the MUP reservists units." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: A correction has been made. It should not say M-U-P, MUP. I think I did make the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but we wanted to do it in court for the record. What is the correction?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It should say "Colonel Milos Djosan." He was a commander of the 52nd Brigade ARBR, and he was responsible for this brigade only, not responsible for MUP reservist units. In that municipality where the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just before -- could you just correct the text first. It says in the second sentence: "Colonel Milos Djosan was also responsible for MUP reservists units." Would it be correct to say that he was responsible for VJ reservist units? Is that the correction you want to make? Could you speak in the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: He was responsible for regular forces and reservist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But not --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The reservists were those people who were mobilised for the needs of the army. They were trained and together with the regular units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll get to that soon, but just let's focus on the text. Is it correct that we should substitute in the second sentence the word -- or the expression VJ for MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Defence counsel, I believe that in the direct examination the Prosecution should not lead the witness, and the Prosecutor is doing that when he is asking whether the word "MUP" should be replaced by "VJ" or the other way around. So could he please put his questions as appropriate in direct examination whether anything should have been changed so that the witness can respond on his own. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In this situation, Mr. Djordjevic, if you look at the answer at page 11, line 4, the witness has already indicated that Colonel Djosan or Djosan was responsible for regular forces and reservist forces; and that they were people who were mobilised for the needs of the army, is at lines 6 and 7. In those circumstances Mr. Stamp, I don't think, is at all leading when he uses the term "VJ," which is the abbreviation for the Yugoslav army, as we have understood it in this trial so far. So I think your point is not well made in this particular case. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Referring back to your previous answers, can I take it, therefore, that in that second sentence in paragraph 6, "VJ" should be substituted for "MUP"?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at paragraph 58 of the statement, please. The third sentence reads that: Prascevic used to be the head of the state security in Gjakove. Is there any change you'd like to make in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: This is not correct. Milutin Prascevic was never a state or public security chief. He was an inspector, and not even a senior inspector, just an inspector. That's what he was, just an inspector, as I said, not a senior inspector in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it from that that the word "chief" in that sentence should be expunged and the word "inspector" --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could turn to paragraph 105 of the statement. Near the end of that paragraph, there's a sentence that reads: "I then went to Ramoc and informed my brother-in-law Pal Gjoklaj and Pal's brother Zef." Is there anything you'd like to change there, do you see there, I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Please, could you repeat that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look to the -- if you look near the end of paragraph 105, you'll see, four sentences from the end, a sentence saying: "I went to Ramoc ..." Was it Ramoc that you went to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Pal Gjoklaj is not my brother-in-law. He is my sister -- he is my wife's brother. So he is the brother of my spouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. And was it Ramoc that you went to and informed him?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And look at the first sentence of paragraph 105. It says that: "The 137th KLA Brigade (about 126 uniformed members and 40 volunteers) at Ramoc were surrounded in early June 1999 ..." Was this at Ramoc?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: A small correction has to be made here, as well, because Ramoc and Madanaj, the places where the people of the 137th Brigade was, this was a mountainous area, and half of it belongs to the Ramoc village and half to the Madanaj village. However, they were mostly in Madanaj. So it's better if it's said here "Madanaj," and I changed it. It should say Madanaj. However, it doesn't make any big a difference, even if you say Ramoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Now, having reviewed your statement dated the 9th of August, 2006, and having made these changes, is the statement otherwise true -- or is the statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if asked about this again, would you make the same declaration that you have made in the statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I would say the same things that have been said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: However, I can add explanations or comments if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Mr. Peraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document marked 02253 -- or the 65 ter 02253 and ask that it be received in evidence under Rule 92 ter as evidence in chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P00313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, there are a couple clarifications and explanations of material in this statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, before I get to that, I recall that the Court had asked that a short -- very short summary be read in respect to the 92 ter witness. This is -- what I read now is just the briefest of outlines in what is a very extensive statement, Your Honours. The evidence of the witness is that he's an ethnic Albanian who during early 1999 was a Captain First Class in the VJ. From December of 1998 until June 1999, he was an officer in the air defence and rocket artillery brigade of the Pristina Corps based in Djakovica. He described in great detail the structure of the VJ, and he also described the structure of the MUP and paramilitary groups, including Arkan's Tigers, Seselj's White Eagles, and Franko Simatovic's unit the Frenchi's -- or Frenki's that were operating in Djakovica in 1998 and particularly during the period March 24 to June 10, 1999. He describes the huge influx of army and police personnel in the Djakovica municipality between February and March 1999, and he also describes that in addition to these units coming into the area, local police units operating in various villages where the regular MUP had difficulty patrolling were also created; that is, in many villages local villagers were enlisted to assist the police as policemen. He further described that sometime in April 1999, in Djakovica municipality, about four policemen were killed in a KLA ambush. Some days thereafter, he was present at a funeral ceremony where there was an informal meeting between senior members of the MUP and the VJ in Djakovica area where it was said and agreed upon that at least 100 Kosovo Albanians would be eliminated and their houses burnt and destroyed in retribution for the killing of the MUP officer in the ambush. He described a large-scale operation which commenced on the 27th of April in the Carragojs or Erenik Trava valley -- Trava river valleys, and this operation continued until the 29th of April, during which a massive massacre of Kosovo Albanian men took place, primarily at police check-points in Meje, Meje-Orize, and Korenica. He describes the position and location of the units of the forces of the FRY involved in the operation. The VJ cordoned off and blocked the valleys from both sides, while VJ and MUP units swept down the valley towards Meje and Djakovica. They burnt property and pushed the Kosovo Albanian villagers down the valley southwards to the check-points, the police check-points that had been set up around Meje. As the Kosovo Albanian population fled down the valley, several convoys were formed, and in the vicinity of Meje, Meje-Orize, and Korenica, the MUP set up check-points where they detained and separated Kosovo Albanian men from the fleeing convoys. Men were summarily executed with members of the MUP from the area participated -- participating in the executions. During these events, the witness and another VJ officer, Seregj Perovic, travelled into the area of operations where they saw several bodies of persons who had been executed, clearly from the injuries that they suffered at the various police check-points. They saw 20 -- over 20 bodies of young men at the Meje-Orize check-point. On the road, they saw bodies of young men scattered. At the two other check-points, I mentioned they saw the bodies of young men who had been shot at close range. They managed with the help of some other VJ members to rescue some persons from execution and also to enable some persons to escape down the mountains or down the valley by helping them passing through check-points or effecting their release from the MUP forces or the forces that had arrested them or held them. The witness also produced some maps which are annotated -- which are attached to his statements. He also said that after the killing, sometime on the 29th on April 1999 while he was on the Meje-Djakovica road, he saw two private civilian trucks driving away from Meje escorted by a police vehicle, each truck containing approximately 20 bodies in circumstances where it is his view that these bodies were being removed for concealment. That, as I indicated, is the briefest of summaries of the evidence contained in the statement of this witness. May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you, Mr. Peraj, just to expand a little bit on some of the matters that you referred to in your statement, and it might assist us if -- if we had before us a map of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I ask that we put on the screen 65 ter document 615.05 -- sorry, 65 ter document 00615.05, and can I ask you to zoom in a little bit at the top left so that Djakovica town goes to the bottom right of the map. Perhaps you could zoom a little bit more, please. A little bit more, taking Djakovica a little bit to the right. That's a little bit too much. Okay. Could we zoom a little more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less. It's good more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You can make out the towns and the area there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Peraj, I'm going to ask you to mark various places on the map, quite a few places. I'm going to ask you to make careful markings, that is to identify where you want to mark before you mark and mark it carefully. Firstly, can you spot on the map where your home village is? Just identify it before you do anything.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: My home village is Ramoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you make it out on the map?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I can't read the font. It is very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Can we -- before you mark anything, can we try to zoom it in one more level to see if we can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that any better? Do you see Ramoc?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can make it out because I know where it is on the map, but it's not clear here. It's blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It's here where I'm pointing with my pen. Dallashaj is here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Can you underline where Ramoc is.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. The witness has put a curved line where Ramoc is indicated on the map. Let's first look at the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to paragraph 65 of your statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please keep the map on. Let us first look at the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You had described the operation. You said in paragraph 65 that the VJ were to the west, and they were also deployed along the Djakovica-Decani road. I'd just like you to mark where the positions of the VJ were during the operation, that is the static positions of the VJ. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can. However, one correction, if I may. The VJ was on both sides of the terrain, both towards the north-east and south-west, so they were on both sides. The army had blocked both sides, and now I can draw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, before you do, can you use carefully unbroken -- sorry, some broken lines to indicate where the army were on the north-west first, where the army positions were blocking on the north-west. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Approximately, the lines, the interrupted lines that I just marked the map with indicate the positions where the army was stationed, how they blocked the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said in paragraph 55 [sic], as well, that: "There were brigade-sized groups including the 63rd Parachute Brigade of about 500 men and a Special Police Brigade of about 400 personnel from Serbia, which pushed down the valley, burning and forcibly displacing civilians toward the paramilitary groups towards Meje." Can you use an arrow to show the direction that the 63rd paramilitary Brigade -- or Parachute Brigade from Nis and the Special Police from Serbia were going?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: This indicates the direction of the attack carried out by the MUP or the police brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the top of that arrow that you just drew, can you just mark "MUP" very -- just indicate that it is the MUP.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You just did it at the bottom. Okay. Okay. Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is writing at the arrow head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which is probably an M. Just so that the record will help us follow it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put another arrow on the map showing the axis of attack of the VJ unit, the 63rd Parachute Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp. I don't read paragraph 65 as saying that the VJ Parachute Brigade was involved in the attack. It was present, but the attack described appears to be one by the Special Police Brigade of about 400 personnel, as I read what is there. I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I should clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you mark, Witness, if we return to paragraph 65 of the statement, and I'll just read it. It says that: "There were brigade-sized groups, including the 36th Parachute Brigade of about 500 men - I do not know the name of the commander - and a Special Police Brigade of about 400 personnel from Serbia, which pushed down the valley, burning and forcibly displacing civilians towards the paramilitary groups around Meje acting as a blocking force." Firstly, the 63rd Parachute Brigade, was that a VJ or a MUP unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It was a VJ unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And which units were pushing down the valley, burning and displacing the civilians?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In a valley, in the north-eastern part of the valley the 63rd Parachute Brigade was there while the MUP was on the other axis. There were trucks, regular police from Gjakove, or reservists. After the convoys left, they set the houses alight. This is the gist of it. These ones, they only drove the people out of their homes, of their houses in the village, and directed them in the direction of the main check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that in the north-eastern part of the valley, the 63rd Parachute Brigade was there. Could you draw a line now, an arrow, carefully showing the axis of attack of the 63rd Parachute Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop, please, Mr. Peraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Chamber has already observed in paragraph 65, they only mention that the 63rd Parachute Brigade was stationed there. You, Your Honour, cautioned my learned friend Mr. Stamp that in this part of the statement, no attack by the 63rd Parachute Brigade is mentioned. That's why I would like to ask the Prosecutor to reformulate his question and to phrase it in accordance with what is written in paragraph 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, paragraph 65 is not clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- if I can phrase it that way, as to whether the 63rd Parachute Brigade was involved in pushing down the valley or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness so far has said that the parachute brigade was at the north-east of the valley and the MUP was on the other axis. It is not yet clear from the witness whether it was the 63rd Brigade which was involved in the push down the valley, perhaps with MUP, or whether it was only the MUP. And once we've got that resolved, I would be grateful if you could also get resolved whether it was these truck-loads of reservists that were involved in the push or whether they merely came along after the push and burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked before, Mr. Peraj, and you answer -- I'll ask you again. Could you name the units or the formation that were involved in the push down the river valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: With full responsibility, I hereby state that in the push, in driving the population out of the population, the Brigade of the police and the 63rd Parachute Brigade from the Nish were involved. They were in the yard of my own house, and after they beat up my father who refused to leave his house, he, my father, said to them, Very well. You, the friends of my son doing this to me. Then the officer from the radio brigade, he had a radio with him, he called Gjakove headquarters to check and verify whether a Nike Peraj was still a VJ member. He received a yes as a reply, and then the people on the ground changed their behaviour towards my family. They did drive them away from the house but said to them that they would be able to come back after two days. I don't know the name of this officer, but I know that his duty was to provide military security in the Brigade. He told me that he had been to my house, and he gave me the name of my father and my mother and described them to me. So this is a fact. Nobody can deny that. At Qafe e Osekut, we've seen this on the map, too, which units were engaged there and the axis of their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: May I provide you with a further clarification, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you clarify first, who or which groups did the burning of the houses? Was it the MUP unit, the 63rd Parachute Brigade of the VJ, or was it the reservists that came later on in trucks?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The special group which followed the army and the police were the ones who burned the house after the terrain was cleansed and the people were moved out. This was a special unit that I saw with my own eyes in Nec, not exactly the same members, but it was the same group where they carried out similar things. Their hands were free to do whatever they wanted. They set the houses on fire and continued downwards. In addition, the 63rd Parachute Brigade did not kill anyone because there wasn't any. They were directed [Realtime transcript read in error, "corrected"] to go to the road. I don't have any knowledge of people being killed on that axis. The people were killed on or near the check-point at Meje and Orize, and totally different units were stationed there on those check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I just see here at line 23 -- sorry, line 12, they were corrected to go to the road. Are you saying that the 63rd Parachute Brigade directed the people to the road?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The Parachute Brigade in the area where it was operating and the police Brigade in its own area of operations, but they were coordinated, the two. The command of the police in Duzhnje and the temporary command at Qafe e Osekut were fully coordinated -- fully coordinated their activities, and I heard it myself on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. So I had asked you earlier if the 63rd -- or I'd asked you which units were involved, and you said the 63rd was on the north-east axis of attack -- or north-west, I beg your pardon. Can you just draw a line, and that will clarify things, I hope, indicating the line of attack of the 63rd Parachute Brigade, an arrow, a line with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It's not the 23rd but the 26th Brigade, to avoid any complications.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 63rd, correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. The witness has drawn another line above -- or another arrow above the first arrow, indicating the axis of movement of the 63rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You had earlier with the broken lines shown where the VJ formations were that were involved in blocking the valley. Do you know what were the names of these formations on the two sides of the valley? Do you know what brigades they were or what units they were?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: On the side where MUP was, including the villages of Orize, Korenica, Meje, Babaj Boks, Shishman, there was a tank battalion from the Prizren Brigade. I think it was the 1st or the 2nd Battalion, tank battalion. A certain Nenad was a security officer in that Brigade. I do not recall the name of the battalion commander at the time, but I know that this battalion even before the war was stationed in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the other side, do you know a unit that was on the other side of the valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: On the other side of the valley was one or two anti-aircraft batteries of my own brigade, the 52nd Rocket Artillery Brigade, and a little but further up in the area of Rastavica and Rec, I think there were some units in that area of Decane and Peja. I'm not quite certain which those units were, but they were army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you heard coordination in respect to the joint operation of the MUP and the VJ on the radio. Where were you when you heard this?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: At Duzhnje, at the forward command post in the Turbe area in Duzhnje. After I returned from Qafe e Osekut, Milan Kotur and Jovica Stankovic were there, and I heard on the radio - the volume was on - about the coordination and to which point they had advanced. He was saying, Continue further up; stop; any resistance? The reply would come, No, not so far, because in fact there was no resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this a forward command post of the VJ or of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It was a command on the ground, on the actual terrain at Turbe. It's called a forward command post or moving command in war-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Was it VJ --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It was MUP. Both the MUP and the VJ commands were moving all the time in order to follow the strategic points, but at Duzhnje was the MUP forward command post, whereas at Qafe e Osekut members or representatives of the forward command post of the brigade in Gjakove and the representatives of the Pristina Corps, that is Milan Kotur, while the representative of my own Brigade was Novica Stankovic. I spent time with them on that occasion. I stayed with them for half an hour and discussed the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Can you see on the map the area where the MUP forward command post was?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It cannot be seen clearly, but it was in the village of Duzhnje. It is the first village just above Korenica. In fact, it is adjacent to Korenica. I can put a dot there if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could put an X there or -- yes, put an X where it is.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It should be here at the point of the arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- yes, the witness has at the point of the arrow written over where he had earlier marked "MUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put an X now where the VJ forward command post was.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the witness has put an X next to the broken lines to the north-west -- sorry, north-east of the markings that he has made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to paragraph 68 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, since I am to move on, I'm wondering if it might be a convenient time, if we could save the markings that the witness has done, and I ask that it be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The marked map will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00314, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We must now, then, have the first break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you to go to paragraph 67 and 68 of your statement. In paragraph 67, you describe where you were on the 27th of April, 1999, and you said sometime in the early afternoon you went with your brother and Major Perovic, I think you said it should be, to the church --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Captain Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you very much. Captain Perovic, to the Catholic church near Boris Kadric Street in Djakovica, and your family was in a tractor near the church, and you found many people from Ramoc village - that's your home village - there. What were they doing there, or why were they there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They had been forced out of their homes and had been told to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in paragraph 68, you said that these persons told you to go to Meje, Meje Hasanaj's house to save some men who had been arrested by the police, and you together with Captain Perovic, you took your family to your apartment in Djakovica, and then you went to Meje. And at Meje-Orize, you stopped at a police check-point. Now, if we could get -- it's P31 for the map you just marked, again on the screen. I would like you to mark where the police check-point was at Meje-Orize, and I would ask, since we are using -- since we are doing so many markings, if we could use a different colour pen on this occasion. The previous pen was red. The previous markings were red. Just put a circle, a small circle, where the police check-point at Meje-Orize was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness has put a black mark, which looks more like a large dot than a circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 69 -- or before we get there, in paragraph 68 you said the MUP inspector Dimitrije Rasovic was in charge of that check-point that you just marked. Did you know MUP Inspector Rasovic before ?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Dimitrije Rasovic is the son of Velisha Rasovic, and they were my neighbours in Dallashaj. However, then they moved to Piskote, close to Gjakove. So I knew him from when he was a little child, and he knows me very well as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said in paragraph 68 that there were also local policemen. How were these policemen dressed? How was Inspector Rasovic and the local policemen dressed?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Regular police uniform. They were from the so-called Special Police at the MUP building in Gjakove. There was a unit that was assigned more special duties than regular policemen, special tasks. They had camouflage uniforms with a blue colour dominating. Correction: The blue colour did not dominate, but that was very similar to the military camouflage uniform, while there were other policemen who had camouflage uniform but where the blue colour was dominating. There were reservist policemen of the MUP who had single-coloured uniforms, which were blue, just blue. There were the so-called local police units, which were mobilised later by the municipality, and they had different uniforms. They used the old uniform of the MUP, the previous one, which was no longer in use by the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What colour was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: There were two or three people with Rasovic there who were only semi-uniformed. They either had police trousers and civilian jackets or the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were these the persons you referred to as paramilitary soldiers in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They, too, wore part of the uniform. They very often, though, would change the uniform they wore. We are speaking here about Orize. In Orize, I did not see paramilitaries. At least, I was not able to see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Or that those persons were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 68 of your statement, you said: "We stopped in Meje-Orize because there was a police check-point. The officer in charge of the check-point was a MUP inspector Dimitrije Rasovic from the village of Piskote. There were also local policemen and paramilitary soldiers at the check-point together with Rasovic." Who are you referring to when you say paramilitary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Maybe the term is not right or has been changed, but paramilitaries were the people who joined the local police and the reservist police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these local police units that you referred to earlier, you said they used the old uniform of the MUP. What colour was that uniform?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Blue. Blue. Not dark blue, lighter blue compared to the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 69, you said you saw four dead bodies lying on the grass behind the toilets of the school where the check-point was. Now, I just want to ask you, how far were these bodies that you saw? How far, the distance between the check-point where the police and Rasovic were and these four bodies?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Not more than 30, 40 -- not 50 metres, no. Just 30 or 40 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Incidentally, how were these policemen that Rasovic was in charge of, how were they armed, if at all? Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I apologise. They had automatic weapons with butts that can be folded. Rasovic had a pistol, 9-millimetre pistol with a magazine of 15 or 16 bullets. The reservists had semi-automatic rifles with a bayonet on top. Some of them had revolvers of TT type, 76 millimetres -- 76.2 millimetres. Some of them also had knives, especially the reservists. I then thought because of these things that they might be paramilitaries because it was them that carried knives most of all, knives that are called daggers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you have described paramilitaries answer in your statement. Can we move quickly, Mr. Peraj, to paragraph 73. You said that you received information - and this is in paragraph 71, I should say - from families that you saw passing in the convoys that men had been killed near Hasanaj's house, and you -- and that was in Meje, and you headed to Meje with Captain Perovic. Now we get to paragraph 73. You said: "We headed towards Meje. When we arrived near Hasanaj's house, we saw people lying on the meadow with their face in the grass. Meje" -- "The person who is Captain Perovic went to speak to the officers at the police check-point in front of Hasanaj's house. I went to the meadow, and there were about 20 dead bodies of men. I turned some of the bodies to see if I could recognise them." Firstly -- well, perhaps we could start with marking. Can you mark where that police check-point was at Meje with a circle.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness has put a circle in -- in -- with a black marker near to the tip or the pointed part of the arrow to the right of his markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How far were these 20 dead men from the police check-point?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The first bodies on the road from the mountain were about 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 74, you say that you saw: "... the faces of the victims devastated. They had been shot from a very close distance in a perfect execution style with automatic rifles. I saw the powder burns on the heads of these victims. They had been shot from vertical positions when they were already on the ground. The policemen at the check-point carried automatic rifles." How were the policemen at this check-point attired?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In the second check-point at Meje, I remember Misko Popovic, somebody with a surname of Isajlovic whom I knew by face, there were some others, as well, who were wearing camouflage uniforms, the same one as Dimitrije Rasovic was wearing in the first check-point. I also saw some other policemen who were wearing camouflage uniforms of the police but where the blue colour was dominant. I am convinced that there I saw paramilitaries from units of the White Eagles, Seselj's White Eagles; Arkan's units, the Tigers; the Frenki units. These people were semi-uniformed. They had blouses or T-shirts on top because it was not very hot at the time. They had painted faces, shaven heads. They carried lion's fangs or teeth around their necks, and on their chests you could see various emblems, their flag which identifies them, and other kinds of emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You describe in paragraph 74, 78 -- or, actually, paragraph 73 to 78 what happened at that check-point, and you said that you had -- yourself and Captain Perovic had a -- had discussions with the police officer Scepanovic in order for them to release some of the men that they were holding. Who was this Scepanovic that you speak of in paragraph 75, 78 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Misko Popovic, Scepanovic, and Isajlovic were there. Perovic knew them very well. He spoke to them. I went to the bodies, and he asked them to release those people. However, he refused to do that. At that time I was looking at the bodies, and an incident happened with a paramilitary soldier. He pointed his gun, his automatic rifle to me. A regular military police soldier was close to me, and he said, Captain, this man is going to kill us; he wants to kill us. I had my automatic rifle on my -- on my left hand, and he said, You're not allowed to be here; leave immediately. I looked at that person, and his trousers -- on the right side of his trousers there were blood streaks. He had a dagger, double-edged dagger, that I am sure he had used to stab people, and then he had wiped the blade on his trousers, on the left side of his trousers. At that moment, I left and went towards Perovic. I told him what was going on. However, before we got to the Meje check-point, close to a rubber factory where they -- where they repair tyres, we ran across about 20 soldiers and a lieutenant who told us where the check-point was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Peraj, thank you for the information. Much of what you have been saying is already recorded in your statement. I just ask you to remember that, and we can't go over all of it again today. I just wanted to ask, Scepanovic, with whom Major Perovic negotiated to effect the release of some of the people who were held at the check-point, did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him from before. I knew him as a face, but I didn't know what his position was, what his tasks were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you said you knew him as a face. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I knew him by face. I knew that his name was Scepanovic, but I had no contacts with him. I didn't know in details what his position was, whether he was employed by the police or whether he worked at the municipality, but on that day the three of them were wearing the same uniform, Isajlovic, Rasovic, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the third name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The third name I think was -- would be Scepanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know Isajlovic and Rasovic before?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I told you about Rasovic. I knew him from when he was a child, from Dallashaj village, and even when he moved to Piskote I visited him in his home on several occasions before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop, stop. Isajlovic, did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Not very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you know him to be a member of the police force?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: What do you mean? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said this is a police check-point and he was there dressed in police uniform. Did you know him to be a police officer, and for how long did you know him to be a police officer?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know how long he had been a policeman until then, but he was there on the spot. There were persons who had worked in the municipality, in the municipal assembly, who had certain functions there and held certain positions. He could have been MUP inspector, too, but that I didn't know then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If you could move to paragraph 79 quickly. You said you left that area because the people in the tractors told you that there were other refugees who needed help, and as you travelled about 600 or 700 metres from Hasanaj's meadow, on the left side of the road you saw four dead bodies lying on the ground, and a pile with other seven dead bodies were lying on the ground a bit further on. They were all men in different ages, from 20 to 50 years old. Can you tell us, in that area where you saw these dead bodies, which, if any, units were present?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: There we didn't see any units. On the lower part of the road, there were some trees there, and two police -- correction, two persons dressed in uniforms showed up. Their uniforms were camouflage ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Military uniforms. They were not shaven, and their hair was long. They hid from us. We had two military policemen with us. We saw the bodies, and from there we returned together with a tractor and another vehicle that was a little bit up. We waved at them, and they came towards us. We escorted them, and they were not stopped at the check-point where we had been previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the people that you escorted through these check-points, who were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: We didn't ask them where they were from, but I think they were from Racaj or Rrypaj village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's further up in the valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Not that further up in comparison with other villages. These villages are about three or four kilometres away from the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After you escorted these people through the check-point, you said from there - and this is paragraph 81 of your statement - you went to Korenica to see if you could help other families, and you saw one dead body near the house of your brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: My sister is married in Korenica, and near their house, on the road, was this body. The family was not there. The whole village had left. The houses were on fire. They had been set alight in the morning, and the flames could still be seen. We attempted to go in the direction of the church in Korenica because we had information that people were blocked there on purpose, deliberately, in the church and that they had been massacred there in the church, but this turned not to be true. There was not a single person in the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were there any check-points in the area of Korenica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. At the entrance to the village by the road there, there was a check-point, but not manned by many. Near this check-point there was a military unit, three, but at the check-point there were three or four policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I -- have a look at that map again, if you can, the map you have been marking, and with the same black pen if you could first identify where the check-point at Korenica was and then put a circle around the place where it was.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It cannot be seen clearly. Somewhere here. Maybe a little bit further up from the place that I marked. Further up. It's further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "up," what do you mean? In which direction?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In the direction of the upper part of the arrow, towards north.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Now, you said that there were convoys of people coming down the valley. Could you use the same marker just to mark where the convoys passed through?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have drawn two black lines which at some point join up at Djakovica, and you have pointed them -- put a pointer away from Djakovica. Where are you indicating that these convoys headed to or went to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I apologise for this line that goes by the village of Korenica. The dotted red line should be outside the direction that I just drew on the map. The convoy coming down from Korenica was heading towards Orize. There, there is a junction, and that's where the two convoys, the convoy that was coming down the Carragojs valley through Meje and the other convoy met. They met at Orize, and they headed in the direction of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And from Gjakove to -- to where? Where did they go after Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In the direction of Albania. Every now and then, the Qafe e Prushit crossing, border crossing was opened, but sometimes it was closed. So that's why everybody was heading in the direction of Gjakove, Prizren, and the border crossing up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that border crossing, the Qafe e Prushit border crossing the only one that was used by the people who were forced out of the valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It was not the only border crossing. Very close to Gjakove, about 12 kilometres away from Gjakove is the Qafe e Prushit border crossing, but it was not regularly opened, and that's why the convoys would pass then through Prizren, Zhur village, and to go to the Morine border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just put an arrow indicating where -- the direction where those people who went to Morine would have travelled.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I cannot see it in the map. I can only see Gjakove at the end of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said earlier that you had made a mistake with the broken red lines that you wanted to use to indicate where the -- the blockading VJ forces were, because the convoy should go within the line. Can you now mark again with the red pointer - if we could get the assistance of the usher - where you now say the unbroken red line showing the blockading VJ forces should be.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness has drawn another unbroken line in the red, slightly to the left of the previous unbroken red line that he had drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I think it's a broken line, you know. Unbroken?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, it is broken. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, having corrected that, and I know it's difficult with this map, can you again look carefully to see where the check-point at Korenica would be?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I cannot read it properly, whether it says Korenica or Koprivnica, though I know the terrain very well. I don't think there is a village Koprivnica there. It was in the middle of the village. I think it's called Korenica Street, Ulica Korenica, the location where it was. It should be here where I'm touching the screen now with my pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just put a cross there. You used the red pen? Could you use a black pen. Could you take the black pen and put a cross where Korenica is.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is where the Korenica check-point was, and I'm not -- a little to the left where you put the circle; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: As I said, it was at the end of the point of the arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. I'd like to take you to the next day, the 28th of April. You said in your statement that yourself and, I think, Captain Perovic travelled up the valley. Did you observe the condition of the houses that were up in the valley and the villages in general?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: From the place where the command was, at Qafe e Osekut, at the time we went there the houses could not be seen because the whole valley was covered in smoke and flames, because the houses were in flames. Especially up in my own village, only one house was still in flames, while in the villages of Rrypaj, Madanaj, all the houses were burning, and for half an hour or so we could not see the houses. Personally, I wanted to see my house and the houses in my village. You can see them very well from that place with the naked eye in other circumstances, but we used binoculars, and that's why I could see that the houses in my village were not burnt down. Although, I thought at the time that only the walls had remained from my houses because the roof -- the roofs of these houses were made of very old tiles, black, dark tiles, but the other houses, not in Dallashaj village, those in Rupaj and Madanaj villages especially, were all burning. The operation was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you leave the command post at Qafe e Osekut and go into the valley itself?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: We were into the valley itself before we went to Qafe e Osekut, and from the valley then we went to Qafe e Osekut.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Thanks for the correction. You said earlier today that there were special groups that came after the 63rd Parachute Brigade and the MUP Special Units that did the burning, and that you saw them at a place called Nec. Well, maybe I have the pronunciation wrong. Where was it that you saw these special groups that were involved with the burning?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, we met them at Nec. They had incendiary material in the trucks, and Perovic instructed them for a house not to be burnt, but this house was burnt, however. It was a special unit, specialised in these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which -- which organisation were they affiliated to? What I'm asking, were they affiliated to the VJ or to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They were affiliated to the MUP, and they were equipped with helmets. They wore helmets on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you speak with any of the -- and that is while you were in the field that day, did you speak with any of the MUP officers in that area on the 28th while you were in the terrain, in the valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't personally, but Perovic did, because the villagers of Meje were stopped at the Meje check-point. At the moment that I and Perovic went there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Could you -- could you --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: -- we met -- will you please allow me to finish it in a few words?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The same persons were there, those that had been there the previous day. It was the whole village of Meje, about 200 persons. So this person said to Perovic, No problem. They will continue their journey. You leave. Have a pleasant journey yourself. So while we were there, we didn't see them ill-treating any of the villagers. They all went downwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The units that you saw or that you said were involved in the burning, the special units, do you know where they were from, where they were based and where they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. When I said special forces, I didn't mean that they were special or experts in something, but they had this special task. They were mainly from the MUP in Gjakove because he knew some of them. They talked. I mean, Perovic knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, in paragraph 65, you said that the Special Police Brigade that was involved in the push down the mountain with the 63rd Parachute Brigade comprised of about 400 personnel from Serbia. This Special Police Brigade that was involved in the original push down the mountain, where in Serbia were they from?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the previous dislocation, whether they were from Belgrade, Nis, or Novi Sad. However, this was a MUP unit from the Republic of Serbia, and when I mention the term "special," I mean that they deal with large-scale operations against terrorism. So they're involved in fighting terrorists, because they wore different uniforms, they had different weaponry that they used, and they are elite units. They are not the normal run-of-the-mill police units. They're more prepared, well trained. I could see this on the ground as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that they had slightly different uniforms. What type of uniforms did these elite units have?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms, including blue, orange, and the brownish colour of leaves in autumn. The design of the uniform was much more sophisticated. They were good-quality uniforms compared to what other people were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were these -- were these units from inside of Kosovo or from outside of Kosovo, from some other part of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't think they came from Serbia directly on those days. I think that they were in Kosovo at the time, and when need arose they came to the place where the forces were gathered. Maybe they were in Peja, in Decane. I don't think they were very far, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that there was a MUP field headquarters, and I think you marked it on the map. Did you go there at any time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: On the 28th of April, in the morning, together with Seregj Perovic, after we received information from this military person near Korenica, we went to the MUP headquarters. They were -- they behaved very correctly towards us. Somebody phoned, and on the 28th they slept there. The night of the 27th and 28th they slept there, and the next day they went towards the place where they would continue with the operation. The next day, a Compangol-type car of the police took us, and we went to the place where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's just focus on the question. So you visited their -- their field headquarters. Did you see there -- or let me ask this way. What was the rank of the MUP officers or ranks of the MUP officers that you saw there when you went there on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I saw at least two persons who were colonels, one lieutenant-colonel, one major, and one general, general of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were all of these people, the two colonels, the lieutenant-colonel, that you just described police officers?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: All of them police officers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know where the general, police general, and the police lieutenant-colonel came from for that operation?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. At least three of them Perovic knew because they talked with each other, and they addressed each other as Chief, Chief. They offered us beer. At that time, it was a rarity to be able to have beer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, certainly -- certainly at that hour of the morning, but how do you know or how did you decide upon the ranks of these people?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They had the rank markings. The general had them on his shoulders. I saw them myself. He had the markings on. In times of war, the ranking is hidden or is not kept, but he had them on. Another thing: The cars they used were special cars, advanced technology. They had an armoured vehicle, which was blue. All their cars were equipped with radio equipment, with long antennas. However, I will say again that Perovic knew them, and he told me, and I quote: They must know that we are from red Gjakove. This is the first time I'm mentioning this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I show you a photograph and ask you to tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I show him P02538. It's a photograph of somebody in a uniform. Oh, I beg your pardon. Before we do that, could we tender -- I'd like to tender this second map, and I ask that it be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you could now have a look at P02538. Could we scroll up a little bit with this one so you could see the full -- not zoom, scroll. Thank you. Could we scroll the map up so we could see the full uniform or the full dress of the person in the photograph, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see here somebody in a type of uniform that -- well, I'll not describe it. Can you tell us what uniform this is that you see depicted here in the person in the foreground of the picture?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: This is a police uniform, or the militia, if you want the other term that we used. It's a camouflage uniform. Blue colour is dominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The person in the photograph also has a --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: He has a gun with a magazine. He's carrying it in his arm. He's also wearing a vest. It's not an anti-bullet vest. It's just to carry these projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I was just about to ask about the vest. You see the vest here with the two pockets at the front with another type of camouflage design. Did you notice anybody that day wearing uniforms with that type of camouflage designs? And when I say that, I mean the 27th or the 28th of April. Camouflage design is -- seems to be a light green but with blue and other colours in it.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I saw these types of uniforms in Meje, in Orize.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these uniforms belonged to which units; do you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Regular police units. But they could have been distributed to reservist units as well. It depends on the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. Yes, I am. I'm very grateful, Your Honour. I'm tendering this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The exhibit contains two photographs. You've dealt with only one. Is that what you're intending?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes. I just intend to tender this one. I should indicate that the second one is just a black and white version of the same photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This one photograph will be the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the document with the ERN number 00326.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have seen this map before, Mr. Peraj, this pre-marked map?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this a map depicting what you described in your statement and in your evidence and which was made from a map that you yourself had drawn before?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Exactly. I have seen this map before, yes, and I handed in this version. I fully agree with whatever has been marked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's one small thing on this map. We see the red lines, which depict the moving convoys. We see that they cross each other. Can you explain that? Or they appear to cross. They may not cross. They appear to cross. Can you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I mentioned it earlier, that in Orize there is a junction.
